\begin{abstract}
Standard confusion-matrix correction for noisy annotations assumes uniform error rates.
When this assumption fails---as it routinely does with LLM classifiers, whose error rates vary by up to $5\times$ across subgroups---correction can reverse the sign of estimated causal effects, concluding a beneficial treatment is harmful.
We derive an exact bias identity for this setting: global correction introduces subgroup-level bias with a product form $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau / (1 - 2\bar{\pi})$, factoring into each subgroup's deviation from the pooled error rate, the treatment effect heterogeneity, and an amplification factor from matrix inversion.
This population-level identity---verified at $R^2 \geq 0.97$ across synthetic grids, semi-synthetic evaluations using 11 empirical LLM confusion matrices, and three structurally distinct CATE estimators---predicts that global correction reverses CATE sign in 14.9\% of configurations at $\tau(0) = 0.03$ and amplifies bias in all eight real LLMs tested.
The identity yields a diagnostic: a condition on per-subgroup error rates alone predicts when correction increases bias, without estimating any treatment effects (AUC $= 1.0$ on subgroups with non-zero $\Delta\tau$; $0.86$ across all synthetic subgroups; $0.63$ on real LLM error profiles).
The per-subgroup correction prescribed by the identity reduces $|\text{bias}|$ by $7.4\times$ via hierarchical Bayesian estimation; when error heterogeneity is insufficient, the diagnostic alone guides practitioners to retain global correction.
\end{abstract}

1	\section{Introduction}
2	\label{sec:intro}
3	
4	Consider estimating whether a content moderation policy reduces hate speech differently across demographic groups, using GPT-4 to classify thousands of posts.
5	After standard confusion-matrix correction, the analysis concludes the policy \emph{increases} hate speech among younger users---but the true effect is protective.
6	This sign reversal is not an edge case.
7	
8	Large language models (LLMs) now routinely replace human annotators in computational social science (CSS), producing labels for sentiment, hate speech, stance, and political discourse at costs orders of magnitude below manual coding~\cite{gilardi2023chatgpt,tornberg2024chatgpt,ziems2024nlp}.
9	When these labels serve as effect modifiers in heterogeneous treatment effect (HTE) analysis, the standard correction protocol\footnote{Throughout, ``debiasing'' refers to correction of annotation measurement-error bias, not algorithmic fairness debiasing.} is straightforward: validate a sample against expert annotations, estimate a confusion matrix, and apply its inverse uniformly to correct conditional average treatment effect (CATE) estimates.
10	Yet LLM annotations are not uniformly accurate: \citet{ashwin2025bias} document misclassification rates varying by up to 5$\times$ across demographic subgroups, consistent with $\Delta\pi > 0.20$ at typical base error rates---well above the $0.15$ threshold at which EC-HTE becomes effective; in our pilot study, GPT-4.1 achieves 85.8\% accuracy on TweetEval sentiment, but error rates range from 10.2\% to 20.0\% across text-feature subgroups ($\Delta\pi = 0.098$).
11	
12	We show that this standard correction can make things worse.
13	In 14.9\% of our synthetic configurations (across a grid of $\Delta\pi$ and $\tau(0)$ values; $\tau(0) = 0.03$), global correction reverses the sign of estimated CATE---a protective treatment ($\tau = +0.03$) appears harmful ($\hat{\tau} = -0.059$)---rising to 31\% at $\tau(0) = 0.01$ (Figure~\ref{fig:sign_reversal}); all eight real LLMs tested amplify bias under global correction, while EC-HTE eliminates sign reversal entirely.
14	Global correction amplifies bias by up to 5.9$\times$ ($K{=}4$ with CausalForest); the classical Frazis-Loeb attenuation correction~\cite{frazis2003estimating} \emph{increases} bias by up to 2.9$\times$.
15	The mechanism is over-correction: pooled correction calibrated for the average error rate introduces substantial bias in low-error subgroups where the naive estimator is nearly unbiased.
16	
17	We derive an exact bias identity explaining when and why this occurs (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}): the correction-induced bias in each subgroup factors into three independently estimable components, verified at $R^2 \geq 0.97$ on synthetic grids and 11 empirical LLM confusion matrices.
18	The identity yields a diagnostic (Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts}) that predicts when global correction will harm a subgroup using only per-subgroup misclassification rates, without estimating any treatment effects (AUC $= 1.0$ on subgroups with non-zero effect heterogeneity; Section~\ref{sec:diagnostic}).
19	
20	The per-subgroup correction prescribed by the identity---implemented via hierarchical Bayesian confusion matrix estimation (EC-HTE)---reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.059 to 0.008 under extreme heterogeneity ($K{=}2$).
21	The advantage is conditional: when $\Delta\pi$ is small, the variance cost of stratification outweighs its bias benefit.
22	
23	Existing corrections---PPI~\cite{angelopoulos2023ppi}, DSL~\cite{egami2024dsl}, PPCI~\cite{sui2026ppci}, arm-specific PPI~\cite{mozer2026ppi}, ForestIV~\cite{bu2023forestiv}---assume homogeneous prediction error; none addresses effect modifier misclassification (Section~\ref{sec:related}).
24	
25	\begin{figure*}[t]
26	\centering
27	\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig1_sign_reversal.pdf}
28	\caption{CATE sign reversal under global correction ($K{=}2$, $\tau(0) = 0.03$). (A) Naive vs.\ global-corrected CATE; red triangles mark sign reversals (7.5\% of subgroup estimates). (B) Extreme case: true $\tau = +0.03$, estimated $\hat{\tau} = -0.059$. (C) 14.9\% of configurations exhibit sign reversal; all 8 real LLMs amplify bias; EC-HTE: 0\% reversal.}
29	\label{fig:sign_reversal}
30	\end{figure*}
31	
32	Our contributions are:
33	\begin{itemize}
34	    \item An exact finite-population bias identity (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}): the bias factors into three independently estimable components ($\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau / (1-2\bar{\pi})$), explaining sign reversal in the LLM annotation setting and enabling the diagnostic below; verified at $R^2 \geq 0.97$ (Sections~\ref{sec:theory},~\ref{sec:bias_mechanism}).
35	    \item An actionable diagnostic (Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts}): a condition on per-subgroup misclassification rates alone predicts when global correction increases bias, without estimating any treatment effects (AUC $= 1.0$ on subgroups with non-zero effect heterogeneity)---independently useful without adopting any specific correction method (Section~\ref{sec:diagnostic}).
36	    \item One corrective instantiation of the identity: per-subgroup hierarchical Bayesian confusion matrix estimation (EC-HTE), compatible with difference-in-means, CausalForest, and R-learner, and composable with PPCI for joint covariate/outcome error---effective when error heterogeneity is sufficient (Sections~\ref{sec:method}--\ref{sec:diagnostic}).
37	\end{itemize}
38	The identity and diagnostic (contributions 1--2) are the primary results, useful without adopting any correction method; EC-HTE is one instantiation showing the identity prescribes effective correction.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

Consider estimating whether a content moderation policy reduces hate speech differently across demographic groups, using GPT-4 to classify thousands of posts.
After standard confusion-matrix correction, the analysis concludes the policy \emph{increases} hate speech among younger users---but the true effect is protective.
This sign reversal is not an edge case.

Large language models (LLMs) now routinely replace human annotators in computational social science (CSS), producing labels for sentiment, hate speech, stance, and political discourse at costs orders of magnitude below manual coding~\cite{gilardi2023chatgpt,tornberg2024chatgpt,ziems2024nlp}.
When these labels serve as effect modifiers in heterogeneous treatment effect (HTE) analysis, the standard correction protocol\footnote{Throughout, ``debiasing'' refers to correction of annotation measurement-error bias, not algorithmic fairness debiasing.} is straightforward: validate a sample against expert annotations, estimate a confusion matrix, and apply its inverse uniformly to correct conditional average treatment effect (CATE) estimates.
Yet LLM annotations are not uniformly accurate: \citet{ashwin2025bias} document misclassification rates varying by up to 5$\times$ across demographic subgroups, consistent with $\Delta\pi > 0.20$ at typical base error rates---well above the $0.15$ threshold at which EC-HTE becomes effective; in our pilot study, GPT-4.1 achieves 85.8\% accuracy on TweetEval sentiment, but error rates range from 10.2\% to 20.0\% across text-feature subgroups ($\Delta\pi = 0.098$).

We show that this standard correction can make things worse.
In 14.9\% of our synthetic configurations (across a grid of $\Delta\pi$ and $\tau(0)$ values; $\tau(0) = 0.03$), global correction reverses the sign of estimated CATE---a protective treatment ($\tau = +0.03$) appears harmful ($\hat{\tau} = -0.059$)---rising to 31\% at $\tau(0) = 0.01$ (Figure~\ref{fig:sign_reversal}); all eight real LLMs tested amplify bias under global correction, while EC-HTE eliminates sign reversal entirely.
Global correction amplifies bias by up to 5.9$\times$ ($K{=}4$ with CausalForest); the classical Frazis-Loeb attenuation correction~\cite{frazis2003estimating} \emph{increases} bias by up to 2.9$\times$.
The mechanism is over-correction: pooled correction calibrated for the average error rate introduces substantial bias in low-error subgroups where the naive estimator is nearly unbiased.

We derive an exact bias identity explaining when and why this occurs (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}): the correction-induced bias in each subgroup factors into three independently estimable components, verified at $R^2 \geq 0.97$ on synthetic grids and 11 empirical LLM confusion matrices.
The identity yields a diagnostic (Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts}) that predicts when global correction will harm a subgroup using only per-subgroup misclassification rates, without estimating any treatment effects (AUC $= 1.0$ on subgroups with non-zero effect heterogeneity; Section~\ref{sec:diagnostic}).

The per-subgroup correction prescribed by the identity---implemented via hierarchical Bayesian confusion matrix estimation (EC-HTE)---reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.059 to 0.008 under extreme heterogeneity ($K{=}2$).
The advantage is conditional: when $\Delta\pi$ is small, the variance cost of stratification outweighs its bias benefit.

Existing corrections---PPI~\cite{angelopoulos2023ppi}, DSL~\cite{egami2024dsl}, PPCI~\cite{sui2026ppci}, arm-specific PPI~\cite{mozer2026ppi}, ForestIV~\cite{bu2023forestiv}---assume homogeneous prediction error; none addresses effect modifier misclassification (Section~\ref{sec:related}).

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig1_sign_reversal.pdf}
\caption{CATE sign reversal under global correction ($K{=}2$, $\tau(0) = 0.03$). (A) Naive vs.\ global-corrected CATE; red triangles mark sign reversals (7.5\% of subgroup estimates). (B) Extreme case: true $\tau = +0.03$, estimated $\hat{\tau} = -0.059$. (C) 14.9\% of configurations exhibit sign reversal; all 8 real LLMs amplify bias; EC-HTE: 0\% reversal.}
\label{fig:sign_reversal}
\end{figure*}

Our contributions are:
\begin{itemize}
    \item An exact finite-population bias identity (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}): the bias factors into three independently estimable components ($\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau / (1-2\bar{\pi})$), explaining sign reversal in the LLM annotation setting and enabling the diagnostic below; verified at $R^2 \geq 0.97$ (Sections~\ref{sec:theory},~\ref{sec:bias_mechanism}).
    \item An actionable diagnostic (Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts}): a condition on per-subgroup misclassification rates alone predicts when global correction increases bias, without estimating any treatment effects (AUC $= 1.0$ on subgroups with non-zero effect heterogeneity)---independently useful without adopting any specific correction method (Section~\ref{sec:diagnostic}).
    \item One corrective instantiation of the identity: per-subgroup hierarchical Bayesian confusion matrix estimation (EC-HTE), compatible with difference-in-means, CausalForest, and R-learner, and composable with PPCI for joint covariate/outcome error---effective when error heterogeneity is sufficient (Sections~\ref{sec:method}--\ref{sec:diagnostic}).
\end{itemize}
The identity and diagnostic (contributions 1--2) are the primary results, useful without adopting any correction method; EC-HTE is one instantiation showing the identity prescribes effective correction.

6	\section{Bias Decomposition: When Debiasing Hurts}
7	\label{sec:theory}
8	
9	We formalize the bias that global misclassification correction introduces when subgroup error rates are heterogeneous.
10	Consider estimating the conditional average treatment effect (CATE) $\tau(z) = \mathbb{E}[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid Z = z]$, where $Z \in \{0, 1\}$ is a binary effect modifier observed only through a noisy annotation $\hat{Z}$.
11	The population consists of $K$ subgroups $S \in \{1, \ldots, K\}$ with weights $w_s = P(S{=}s)$, each characterized by a $2 \times 2$ confusion matrix $C_s$ with symmetric error rate $\pi_s = P(\hat{Z} \neq Z \mid S{=}s)$.
12	Standard practice estimates a single confusion matrix $\bar{C} = \sum_s w_s C_s$ from expert annotations and applies its inverse uniformly to all observations, with pooled error rate $\bar{\pi} = \sum_s w_s \pi_s$.
13	We show that when error rates vary across subgroups, this global procedure introduces a bias with an exact product form.
14	
15	We state five assumptions maintained throughout.
16	%
17	\begin{itemize}
18	\item[\textbf{(A1)}] \textit{Conditional independence:} misclassification depends only on the true label $Z$ and subgroup $S$, not on potential outcomes $Y(0), Y(1)$.
19	\item[\textbf{(A2)}] \textit{Symmetric misclassification:} $P(\hat{Z}{=}1 \mid Z{=}0, S{=}s) = P(\hat{Z}{=}0 \mid Z{=}1, S{=}s) = \pi_s$ for all $s$ (diagnostic only; see Remark~2).
20	\item[\textbf{(A3)}] \textit{Balanced effect modifier:} $P(Z{=}0) = P(Z{=}1) = 0.5$. This simplifies the exposition; we discuss relaxation below.
21	\item[\textbf{(A4)}] \textit{Non-degeneracy:} $\pi_s \neq 0.5$ for all $s$, ensuring each $C_s$ is invertible.
22	\item[\textbf{(A5)}] \textit{Homogeneous treatment effects across subgroups:} $\tau(z, s) = \tau(z)$ for all $s$, so $\Delta\tau = \tau(1) - \tau(0)$ is a scalar.
23	\end{itemize}
24	
25	Under (A2)--(A3), the Bayesian mixing matrix $M_s$ (entries $M_s[\hat{z}, z] = P(Z{=}z \mid \hat{Z}{=}\hat{z}, S{=}s)$) coincides with $C_s$.
26	The global mixing matrix is $M_{\text{global}} = \sum_s w_s M_s$.
27	
28	\begin{theorem}[Bias Decomposition Identity]
29	\label{thm:bias_identity}
30	Under \textnormal{(A1)--(A5)}, the bias of global correction in subgroup $s$ at effect-modifier level $z$ is
31	\begin{align}
32	\mathrm{bias}_{\mathrm{global}}(z{=}0, s) &= +\frac{\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau}{1 - 2\bar{\pi}}, \label{eq:bias_z0} \\
33	\mathrm{bias}_{\mathrm{global}}(z{=}1, s) &= -\frac{\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau}{1 - 2\bar{\pi}}, \label{eq:bias_z1}
34	\end{align}
35	where $\delta_s = \pi_s - \bar{\pi}$ is the subgroup deviation from the pooled error rate and $\Delta\tau = \tau(1) - \tau(0)$ is the CATE heterogeneity.
36	\end{theorem}
37	
38	Equations~\eqref{eq:bias_z0}--\eqref{eq:bias_z1} constitute an exact finite-population identity, not an asymptotic approximation or bound.
39	The bias factors into three interpretable components: $\delta_s$ captures how much subgroup $s$ deviates from the average misclassification rate, $\Delta\tau$ captures treatment effect heterogeneity across levels of $Z$, and $1/(1 - 2\bar{\pi})$ is an amplification factor from matrix inversion.
40	Bias vanishes when either source of variation is absent ($\delta_s = 0$ or $\Delta\tau = 0$), and arises only through their interaction.
41	Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} implies that global correction trades one source of confounding for another: it removes attenuation from label noise but introduces a new bias from error-rate heterogeneity.
42	
43	\paragraph{Proof sketch.}
44	Global correction applies $M_{\text{global}}^{-1}$ to the subgroup-specific observed CATE $\tau_{\text{obs}}(\cdot, s) = M_s \cdot \tau_{\text{true}}$, yielding bias $(M_{\text{global}}^{-1} M_s - I) \cdot \tau_{\text{true}}$.
45	Direct computation shows $M_{\text{global}}^{-1} M_s - I = \frac{\delta_s}{1-2\bar{\pi}} \bigl[\begin{smallmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{smallmatrix}\bigr]$.
46	Applying this matrix to $[\tau(0),\, \tau(1)]^\top$ produces the product form.
47	The full derivation appears in Appendix~\ref{app:derivation}.
48	For comparison with classical scalar attenuation~\citep{frazis2003estimating}, see Section~\ref{sec:related}.
49	
50	\paragraph{Relationship to classical scalar attenuation.}
51	Classical scalar attenuation~\citep{frazis2003estimating} gives $\beta^* = \beta(1 - 2\pi)$; dividing by $(1 - 2\bar{\pi})$ removes this bias under homogeneous errors, but Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} characterizes a structurally distinct quantity: \emph{correction-induced} bias from applying $M_{\mathrm{global}}^{-1}$ to heterogeneous $M_s$.
52	F-L scalar correction (dividing $\hat{\tau}(z)$ by $1 - 2\bar{\pi}$) over-corrects low-error and under-corrects high-error subgroups---the same mechanism as global CM correction but restricted to a scalar ignoring the mixing structure between $z$-levels.
53	When $\pi_s \to 0.5$, $(1 - 2\pi_s) \to 0$ and the F-L per-subgroup correction diverges; EC-HTE's $\kappa$-guard (Section~\ref{sec:method}) avoids this singularity.
54	Table~\ref{tab:main_results} confirms: under extreme heterogeneity ($K{=}2$), the classical F-L scalar correction \emph{increases} $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.058 to 0.122 ($2.1\times$ naive), and F-L per-subgroup to 0.168 ($2.9\times$)---the textbook attenuation correction systematically amplifies bias when subgroup error rates differ.
55	
56	\begin{remark}
57	Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} does not require assumption~(A2).
58	For arbitrary asymmetric confusion matrices ($\mathrm{FPR}_s \neq \mathrm{FNR}_s$),
59	the product form $\mathrm{bias}(z, s) = \Delta\tau \cdot [B_s]_{z,1}$ holds exactly,
60	where $B_s = M_{\mathrm{global}}^{-1} M_s - I$, because $B_s \mathbf{1} = \mathbf{0}$
61	follows from stochasticity of $M_s$ and $M_{\mathrm{global}}$ alone.
62	Assumption~(A2) simplifies $[B_s]_{z,1}$ to the scalar
63	$\pm \delta_s / (1 - 2\bar{\pi})$ but is not necessary for the product structure.
64	Under asymmetric errors, the diagnostic (Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts}) requires evaluating $[B_s]_{z,1}$ cell-by-cell rather than via a single scalar threshold; the AUC decreases from 0.86 to 0.66 (Appendix~\ref{app:asymmetric}), reflecting the additional complexity of cell-specific error rates.
65	For binary effect modifiers ($|\mathcal{Z}|{=}2$), the asymmetric score $|[B_s]_{z,1}|$ reduces to a monotone transform of the symmetric score $|\delta_s|/((1{-}2\bar{\pi})\pi_s)$, because column-stochastic $M$ forces $|B_s[0,1]|{=}|B_s[1,1]|$; practitioners may use the simpler symmetric formula without loss.
66	See Appendix~\ref{app:asymmetric} for the full derivation and empirical verification
67	($R^2 = 0.991$).
68	\end{remark}
69	
70	\begin{proposition}[Exact Identity under Heterogeneous Treatment Effects]
71	\label{prop:a5_relaxation}
72	When $\tau(z, s)$ varies across subgroups (relaxing A5), the bias identity remains exact:
73	\begin{equation}
74	\mathrm{bias}_{\mathrm{global}}(z{=}0, s) = +\frac{\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau_s}{1 - 2\bar{\pi}}, \quad
75	\mathrm{bias}_{\mathrm{global}}(z{=}1, s) = -\frac{\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau_s}{1 - 2\bar{\pi}},
76	\end{equation}
77	where $\Delta\tau_s = \tau_s(1) - \tau_s(0)$ is the subgroup-specific CATE heterogeneity.
78	\end{proposition}
79	
80	\begin{corollary}[Aggregate Bias]
81	\label{cor:aggregate_bias}
82	The population-weighted aggregate bias is $\mathrm{Cov}_w(\pi_s, \Delta\tau_s) / (1 - 2\bar{\pi})$.
83	\end{corollary}
84	
85	The proof is immediate: $B_s = M_{\mathrm{global}}^{-1} M_s - I$ depends only on confusion matrices, not on $\tau$.
86	The diagnostic (Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts}) extends unchanged: $\Delta\tau_s$ cancels, so~\eqref{eq:hurts_condition} remains $\Delta\tau$-free.
87	EC-HTE maintains $\geq$93\% coverage under both positive and negative $\Delta\tau_s$--$\delta_s$ correlation (Appendix~\ref{app:a5_violation}).
88	
89	The identity extends to $K > 2$ subgroups with $J$ effect-modifier levels; the multi-class bias retains the same product structure with modified amplification terms (Corollary~\ref{cor:multiclass} in Appendix~\ref{app:multiclass}).
90	
91	Assumption~(A3) ensures $M_s = C_s$; when $P(Z{=}1) \neq 0.5$, the mixing matrices acquire asymmetric entries, but the product structure persists with modified coefficients (Appendix~\ref{app:derivation}).
92	Empirical verification under class imbalance (Appendix~\ref{app:classimbalance}) shows $R^2 \geq 0.976$ even at $P(Z{=}1) = 0.1$ for $K{=}2$, though EC-HTE's RMSE ratio relative to global correction increases to 1.06--1.68 as imbalance grows.
93	Empirical verification (Section~\ref{sec:bias_mechanism}) yields $R^2 = 0.994$ for $K{=}2$ and $R^2 = 0.97$ for $K{=}4$, closing the theory-practice gap to essentially zero; the residual variance reflects Monte Carlo noise, not model misspecification.
94	
95	\paragraph{Sensitivity to (A1).}
96	Assumption~(A1) is not empirically testable.
97	If misclassification correlates with potential outcomes ($\gamma = \mathrm{Corr}(\mathbb{1}[\hat{Z} {\neq} Z],\, Y(1){-}Y(0) \mid Z, S) \neq 0$), Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} gains an $O(\gamma)$ perturbation; in NLP settings, this is plausible when LLM accuracy varies with outcome magnitude.
98	At $\gamma_T = 0.10$, EC-HTE coverage degrades to 75\%; sensitivity analysis frameworks~\cite{lash2009applying,dorn2022sharp,cinelli2020making} can bound the degradation (Section~\ref{sec:limitations}).
99	
100	\paragraph{Finite-sample remainder.}
101	Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} is a population-level identity.
102	In practice, confusion matrices are estimated from $n_{\text{expert}}$ expert labels with $\hat{C}_s = C_s + E_s$, $\|E_s\| = O_p(n_{\text{expert}}^{-1/2})$; the resulting remainder is therefore $R_n = O_p(n_{\text{expert}}^{-1/2} \cdot \kappa(C_s))$, motivating the singularity guard ($\kappa > 100 \to$ fallback) in Section~\ref{sec:method}.
103	
104	\begin{proposition}[Debiasing Can Increase Bias]
105	\label{prop:debiasing_hurts}
106	Under \textnormal{(A1)--(A5)}, global correction produces larger absolute bias than the naive estimator ($|\mathrm{bias}_{\mathrm{global}}| > |\mathrm{bias}_{\mathrm{naive}}|$) in subgroup $s$ if and only if
107	\begin{equation}
108	\frac{|\delta_s|}{(1 - 2\bar{\pi}) \cdot \pi_s} > 1.
109	\label{eq:hurts_condition}
110	\end{equation}
111	\end{proposition}
112	
113	Equation~\eqref{eq:hurts_condition} partitions subgroups into two regimes:
114	\begin{itemize}
115	    \item \textit{High-error} ($\pi_s > \bar{\pi}$): the condition reduces to $\pi_s > 0.5$, excluded by~(A4); global correction always reduces bias.
116	    \item \textit{Low-error} ($\pi_s < \bar{\pi}$): the condition holds whenever $\pi_s < \bar{\pi} / (2(1 - \bar{\pi}))$---easily satisfied: when $\bar{\pi} = 0.15$, any subgroup with $\pi_s < 0.088$ is harmed by global correction.
117	\end{itemize}
118	The mechanism is over-correction: for subgroups with near-zero misclassification ($\pi_s \approx 0$), the naive estimator is nearly unbiased, yet global inversion calibrated for $\bar{\pi}$ creates substantial bias---debiasing is worse than doing nothing, and can reverse bias sign across subgroups.
119	
120	In our experiments (Section~\ref{sec:bias_mechanism}), global correction increases bias in 50\% of $K{=}2$ configurations (260/520), with amplification reaching $2.86\times$ ($K{=}2$) and $2.41\times$ ($K{=}4$); Figure~\ref{fig:heatmap} visualizes the full parameter grid.

1	\section{Correction Prescribed by the Identity}
2	\label{sec:method}
3	
4	Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} identifies per-subgroup misclassification deviation as the bias source; the natural correction is per-subgroup confusion matrix inversion.
5	This correction (EC-HTE) proceeds in three stages: estimate per-subgroup confusion matrices via hierarchical Bayes, invert them to correct observed outcome moments, and propagate correction uncertainty into downstream causal estimators.
6	The complete procedure is summarized in Algorithm~\ref{alg:echte} (Appendix~\ref{app:algorithm}).
7	
8	\subsection{Hierarchical Bayes Confusion Matrix Estimation}
9	
10	We place a Dirichlet-Multinomial hierarchical model over the confusion matrices $\{C_s\}_{s=1}^K$.
11	For each subgroup $s$, row $j$ of $C_s$ has a Dirichlet prior centered at the global pooled confusion matrix $\hat{C}_{\text{global}}$: $\text{Dir}(\alpha_0 \cdot \hat{C}_{\text{global},j})$, where $\hat{C}_{\text{global},j}$ is the $j$-th row of the pooled CM and $\alpha_0 > 0$ is a shared concentration parameter estimated via empirical Bayes (marginal likelihood maximization).
12	We place a $\mathrm{Gamma}(a_0, b_0)$ hyperprior on $\alpha_0$ with defaults $a_0 = 3$, $b_0 = 1$, robust to $2\times$ perturbation of $(a_0, b_0)$ (RMSE change $\leq 4\%$; Appendix~\ref{app:dgp}).
13	Large $\alpha_0$ pulls subgroup estimates toward $\hat{C}_{\text{global}}$ (global correction), while small $\alpha_0$ allows subgroup-specific rates to dominate (stratified correction).
14	This partial pooling---a form of James-Stein shrinkage well-established in small-area estimation---borrows strength across subgroups when estimating confusion matrices from limited expert labels, reducing variance for small subgroups while preserving heterogeneity where data support it.
15	
16	Posterior inference uses centered empirical Bayes optimization ($<$5ms for $K{=}4$, $N{=}5{,}000$); a full Gibbs MCMC alternative requires $\sim$5s (convergence diagnostics in Appendix~\ref{app:algorithm}).
17	Bootstrap SE ($B{=}100$) adds $\sim$0.4s.
18	HB estimation outperforms stratified MLE in 87.5\% of configurations (21 of 24) across the experimental grid (Section~\ref{sec:ec_hte_eval}), with the largest gains when $n_{\text{expert}} / K < 100$.
19	The advantage requires $n_{\text{expert}} \times P(Z_{\text{minority}}) / K \geq 25$ per subgroup; below this threshold, stratified MLE is preferred because the hierarchical model lacks sufficient observations for stable shrinkage.
20	At $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 1000$, HB and stratified MLE converge to within 0.5\% on all metrics.
21	Sensitivity analysis shows $<$5\% RMSE variation under 2$\times$ hyperprior perturbation, confirming that results are not driven by prior specification.
22	
23	\subsection{Subgroup-Stratified Correction}
24	
25	Given posterior mean confusion matrices $\hat{C}_s$, we correct observed outcome moments per subgroup by matrix inversion:
26	\begin{equation}
27	\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_s = \hat{C}_s^{-1} \cdot \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_s,
28	\end{equation}
29	where $\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_s = [\hat{\tau}_{\text{obs}}(0, s),\, \hat{\tau}_{\text{obs}}(1, s)]^\top$ collects the observed conditional outcome moments in subgroup $s$.
30	This requires $\det(\hat{C}_s) \neq 0$ for all $s$, which holds under assumption~(A4) ($\pi_s \neq 0.5$) but may fail in finite samples when error rates approach degeneracy.
31	In practice, Laplace smoothing of the confusion matrix counts ensures finite-sample invertibility.
32	We impose a singularity guard: if the condition number $\kappa(\hat{C}_s) > 100$ (for a $2{\times}2$ symmetric confusion matrix, this corresponds to $\pi_s > 0.495$, i.e., near-random classification), subgroup $s$ falls back to global correction $\bar{C}^{-1}$; when the fallback triggers, the standard error computation also uses $\bar{C}^{-1}$ for that subgroup, ensuring consistency between point estimates and confidence intervals.
33	This hard guard prevents numerical catastrophe; $\kappa \leq 1.25$ is a sufficient condition for strongest bias reduction (Appendix~\ref{sec:budget}), though EC-HTE maintains calibrated coverage ($\geq$93\%) across the wider $\kappa \in [1.4, 3.0]$ range observed in practice (Appendix~\ref{app:kappa_analysis}).
34	
35	The contrast with global correction is direct.
36	Global correction applies $\bar{C}^{-1}$ uniformly to all subgroups, introducing the $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau$ bias identified in Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}.
37	Subgroup-stratified correction eliminates this bias by matching each subgroup's correction to its own misclassification structure, at the cost of higher variance from estimating $K$ separate confusion matrices (Appendix~\ref{sec:budget}).
38	
39	\subsection{Variance-Adjusted CausalForest}
40	
41	For heterogeneous treatment effect estimation, we feed corrected covariates into CausalForestDML~\cite{wager2018causal} with honest splitting.
42	The forest produces per-observation standard error estimates $\text{se}_i$.
43	To account for confusion matrix correction, we propagate uncertainty through the inverse mapping:
44	\begin{equation}
45	\text{se}_{\text{corrected},i} = \sqrt{\text{diag}\!\left(\hat{C}_{S_i}^{-1}\, \text{diag}(\text{se}_i^2)\, \hat{C}_{S_i}^{-\top}\right)}.
46	\end{equation}
47	This plug-in SE conditions on $\hat{C}_s$, neglecting CM estimation uncertainty; at $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 100$ this is negligible, but below this threshold a full bootstrap ($B{=}100$; re-estimate CM and re-fit per replicate) maintains $\geq$95\% coverage across all budgets tested ($n_{\text{expert}} \in \{25, 50, 75, 100, 200\}$); even plug-in SE achieves $\geq$91\% at $n_{\text{expert}}{=}25$ (Appendix~\ref{app:bootstrap_se}).
48	When $n_{\text{expert}}/K < 50$, we recommend bootstrap SE; otherwise plug-in SE suffices.
49	
50	\paragraph{Diagnostic criterion.}
51	Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts} provides a $\Delta\tau$-free diagnostic: global correction harms subgroup $s$ if and only if $|\delta_s| / ((1-2\bar{\pi}) \cdot \pi_s) > 1$, a condition depending only on per-subgroup misclassification rates estimable from a pilot sample.
52	This breaks the circular dependency that would arise if the diagnostic required CATE estimates.
53	A threshold classifier achieves AUC~=~0.86 at the subgroup level, reaching 1.0 when restricted to subgroups with $\tau_s > 0$ (Section~\ref{sec:diagnostic}).
54	
55	\paragraph{Composition with PPCI.}
56	EC-HTE corrects structured covariate misclassification through $\hat{C}_s^{-1}$ inversion but cannot address outcome-level measurement error.
57	PPCI~\cite{sui2026ppci} corrects residual outcome bias using a debiasing estimator but assumes correct covariate labels.
58	The two methods are complementary: apply EC-HTE first to correct covariate labels, then PPCI to correct outcome predictions.
59	Neither is redundant with the other: EC-HTE alone cannot fix outcome error, while PPCI alone incurs higher variance for covariate error.
60	Under both error types simultaneously, the composition reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.179 to 0.007 (Appendix~\ref{sec:ppci}).
61	The two methods target different error sources and are not substitutes: under covariate-side error alone (DGP~A), EC-HTE provides a 27\% RMSE advantage over PPCI; under outcome-side error alone (DGP~C), PPCI achieves $|\text{bias}| = 0.003$--$0.004$ and EC-HTE's marginal contribution is negligible.

\section{Correction Prescribed by the Identity}
\label{sec:method}

Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} identifies per-subgroup misclassification deviation as the bias source; the natural correction is per-subgroup confusion matrix inversion.
This correction (EC-HTE) proceeds in three stages: estimate per-subgroup confusion matrices via hierarchical Bayes, invert them to correct observed outcome moments, and propagate correction uncertainty into downstream causal estimators.
The complete procedure is summarized in Algorithm~\ref{alg:echte} (Appendix~\ref{app:algorithm}).

\subsection{Hierarchical Bayes Confusion Matrix Estimation}

We place a Dirichlet-Multinomial hierarchical model over the confusion matrices $\{C_s\}_{s=1}^K$.
For each subgroup $s$, row $j$ of $C_s$ has a Dirichlet prior centered at the global pooled confusion matrix $\hat{C}_{\text{global}}$: $\text{Dir}(\alpha_0 \cdot \hat{C}_{\text{global},j})$, where $\hat{C}_{\text{global},j}$ is the $j$-th row of the pooled CM and $\alpha_0 > 0$ is a shared concentration parameter estimated via empirical Bayes (marginal likelihood maximization).
We place a $\mathrm{Gamma}(a_0, b_0)$ hyperprior on $\alpha_0$ with defaults $a_0 = 3$, $b_0 = 1$, robust to $2\times$ perturbation of $(a_0, b_0)$ (RMSE change $\leq 4\%$; Appendix~\ref{app:dgp}).
Large $\alpha_0$ pulls subgroup estimates toward $\hat{C}_{\text{global}}$ (global correction), while small $\alpha_0$ allows subgroup-specific rates to dominate (stratified correction).
This partial pooling---a form of James-Stein shrinkage well-established in small-area estimation---borrows strength across subgroups when estimating confusion matrices from limited expert labels, reducing variance for small subgroups while preserving heterogeneity where data support it.

Posterior inference uses centered empirical Bayes optimization ($<$5ms for $K{=}4$, $N{=}5{,}000$); a full Gibbs MCMC alternative requires $\sim$5s (convergence diagnostics in Appendix~\ref{app:algorithm}).
Bootstrap SE ($B{=}100$) adds $\sim$0.4s.
HB estimation outperforms stratified MLE in 87.5\% of configurations (21 of 24) across the experimental grid (Section~\ref{sec:ec_hte_eval}), with the largest gains when $n_{\text{expert}} / K < 100$.
The advantage requires $n_{\text{expert}} \times P(Z_{\text{minority}}) / K \geq 25$ per subgroup; below this threshold, stratified MLE is preferred because the hierarchical model lacks sufficient observations for stable shrinkage.
At $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 1000$, HB and stratified MLE converge to within 0.5\% on all metrics.
Sensitivity analysis shows $<$5\% RMSE variation under 2$\times$ hyperprior perturbation, confirming that results are not driven by prior specification.

\subsection{Subgroup-Stratified Correction}

Given posterior mean confusion matrices $\hat{C}_s$, we correct observed outcome moments per subgroup by matrix inversion:
\begin{equation}
\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_s = \hat{C}_s^{-1} \cdot \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_s,
\end{equation}
where $\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_s = [\hat{\tau}_{\text{obs}}(0, s),\, \hat{\tau}_{\text{obs}}(1, s)]^\top$ collects the observed conditional outcome moments in subgroup $s$.
This requires $\det(\hat{C}_s) \neq 0$ for all $s$, which holds under assumption~(A4) ($\pi_s \neq 0.5$) but may fail in finite samples when error rates approach degeneracy.
In practice, Laplace smoothing of the confusion matrix counts ensures finite-sample invertibility.
We impose a singularity guard: if the condition number $\kappa(\hat{C}_s) > 100$ (for a $2{\times}2$ symmetric confusion matrix, this corresponds to $\pi_s > 0.495$, i.e., near-random classification), subgroup $s$ falls back to global correction $\bar{C}^{-1}$; when the fallback triggers, the standard error computation also uses $\bar{C}^{-1}$ for that subgroup, ensuring consistency between point estimates and confidence intervals.
This hard guard prevents numerical catastrophe; $\kappa \leq 1.25$ is a sufficient condition for strongest bias reduction (Appendix~\ref{sec:budget}), though EC-HTE maintains calibrated coverage ($\geq$93\%) across the wider $\kappa \in [1.4, 3.0]$ range observed in practice (Appendix~\ref{app:kappa_analysis}).

The contrast with global correction is direct.
Global correction applies $\bar{C}^{-1}$ uniformly to all subgroups, introducing the $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau$ bias identified in Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}.
Subgroup-stratified correction eliminates this bias by matching each subgroup's correction to its own misclassification structure, at the cost of higher variance from estimating $K$ separate confusion matrices (Appendix~\ref{sec:budget}).

\subsection{Variance-Adjusted CausalForest}

For heterogeneous treatment effect estimation, we feed corrected covariates into CausalForestDML~\cite{wager2018causal} with honest splitting.
The forest produces per-observation standard error estimates $\text{se}_i$.
To account for confusion matrix correction, we propagate uncertainty through the inverse mapping:
\begin{equation}
\text{se}_{\text{corrected},i} = \sqrt{\text{diag}\!\left(\hat{C}_{S_i}^{-1}\, \text{diag}(\text{se}_i^2)\, \hat{C}_{S_i}^{-\top}\right)}.
\end{equation}
This plug-in SE conditions on $\hat{C}_s$, neglecting CM estimation uncertainty; at $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 100$ this is negligible, but below this threshold a full bootstrap ($B{=}100$; re-estimate CM and re-fit per replicate) maintains $\geq$95\% coverage across all budgets tested ($n_{\text{expert}} \in \{25, 50, 75, 100, 200\}$); even plug-in SE achieves $\geq$91\% at $n_{\text{expert}}{=}25$ (Appendix~\ref{app:bootstrap_se}).
When $n_{\text{expert}}/K < 50$, we recommend bootstrap SE; otherwise plug-in SE suffices.

\paragraph{Diagnostic criterion.}
Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts} provides a $\Delta\tau$-free diagnostic: global correction harms subgroup $s$ if and only if $|\delta_s| / ((1-2\bar{\pi}) \cdot \pi_s) > 1$, a condition depending only on per-subgroup misclassification rates estimable from a pilot sample.
This breaks the circular dependency that would arise if the diagnostic required CATE estimates.
A threshold classifier achieves AUC~=~0.86 at the subgroup level, reaching 1.0 when restricted to subgroups with $\tau_s > 0$ (Section~\ref{sec:diagnostic}).

\paragraph{Composition with PPCI.}
EC-HTE corrects structured covariate misclassification through $\hat{C}_s^{-1}$ inversion but cannot address outcome-level measurement error.
PPCI~\cite{sui2026ppci} corrects residual outcome bias using a debiasing estimator but assumes correct covariate labels.
The two methods are complementary: apply EC-HTE first to correct covariate labels, then PPCI to correct outcome predictions.
Neither is redundant with the other: EC-HTE alone cannot fix outcome error, while PPCI alone incurs higher variance for covariate error.
Under both error types simultaneously, the composition reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.179 to 0.007 (Appendix~\ref{sec:ppci}).
The two methods target different error sources and are not substitutes: under covariate-side error alone (DGP~A), EC-HTE provides a 27\% RMSE advantage over PPCI; under outcome-side error alone (DGP~C), PPCI achieves $|\text{bias}| = 0.003$--$0.004$ and EC-HTE's marginal contribution is negligible.

1	\section{Experiments}
2	
3	\subsection{Setup}
4	
5	We test on synthetic ($N{=}5{,}000$, $K \in \{2, 4\}$, controlled $\Delta\tau$ and $\Delta\pi$, 100 MC runs) and semi-synthetic (TweetEval sentiment~\cite{barbieri2020tweeteval}, $K{=}4$ unbalanced subgroups, $\pi \in \{0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.25\}$) DGPs; full specifications in Appendix~\ref{app:dgp}.
6	
7	We compare: (1) \textit{Naive} (no correction), (2) \textit{Global} (pooled confusion matrix, equivalent to PPI/DSL~\cite{angelopoulos2023ppi,egami2024dsl} with homogeneous error), (3) \textit{Stratified MLE} (per-subgroup DSL without shrinkage), (4) \textit{HB EC-HTE} (per-subgroup correction), (5) \textit{PPCI}~\cite{sui2026ppci}, and (6) \textit{EC-HTE+PPCI}.
8	For CausalForest~\cite{wager2018causal}, we compare naive, global, and EC-HTE variants.
9	Primary metrics are $|\text{bias}|$, RMSE, and 95\% CI coverage, averaged across subgroups and 100 MC runs.
10	Robustness validation covers hate speech, six OpenAI models, subgroup misspecification, asymmetric confusion matrices, confounded treatment, outcome-dependent misclassification (all $\geq$93.5\% coverage), and treatment-dependent misclassification ($\approx$90\% at $\gamma_T \leq 0.05$; Appendices~\ref{app:hatespeech}--\ref{app:treatment_dep}).

\section{Experiments}

\subsection{Setup}

We test on synthetic ($N{=}5{,}000$, $K \in \{2, 4\}$, controlled $\Delta\tau$ and $\Delta\pi$, 100 MC runs) and semi-synthetic (TweetEval sentiment~\cite{barbieri2020tweeteval}, $K{=}4$ unbalanced subgroups, $\pi \in \{0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.25\}$) DGPs; full specifications in Appendix~\ref{app:dgp}.

We compare: (1) \textit{Naive} (no correction), (2) \textit{Global} (pooled confusion matrix, equivalent to PPI/DSL~\cite{angelopoulos2023ppi,egami2024dsl} with homogeneous error), (3) \textit{Stratified MLE} (per-subgroup DSL without shrinkage), (4) \textit{HB EC-HTE} (per-subgroup correction), (5) \textit{PPCI}~\cite{sui2026ppci}, and (6) \textit{EC-HTE+PPCI}.
For CausalForest~\cite{wager2018causal}, we compare naive, global, and EC-HTE variants.
Primary metrics are $|\text{bias}|$, RMSE, and 95\% CI coverage, averaged across subgroups and 100 MC runs.
Robustness validation covers hate speech, six OpenAI models, subgroup misspecification, asymmetric confusion matrices, confounded treatment, outcome-dependent misclassification (all $\geq$93.5\% coverage), and treatment-dependent misclassification ($\approx$90\% at $\gamma_T \leq 0.05$; Appendices~\ref{app:hatespeech}--\ref{app:treatment_dep}).
Semi-synthetic evaluation uses empirical LLM confusion matrices from 16 model--dataset--$K$ combinations (8 LLMs $\times$ 2 datasets $\times$ varying $K$); of these, 11 have sufficient subgroup variation for $R^2$ regression and 13 have $K{=}4$ for $\kappa$ analysis.

\subsection{Empirical Validation of the Bias Identity}
\label{sec:bias_mechanism}

We verify Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} on a $K{=}2$ grid (520 configurations, $\Delta\pi \in [0, 0.25]$, $\Delta\tau \in (0, 0.50]$) and a $K{=}4$ grid (Appendix~\ref{app:dgp}).
Regressing observed subgroup bias on $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau / (1{-}2\bar{\pi})$ yields $R^2 = 0.994$ ($K{=}2$) and $0.97$ ($K{=}4$); residual variance reflects MC noise ($R^2 \geq 0.976$ even at $P(Z{=}1) = 0.1$; Appendix~\ref{app:classimbalance}).
Global correction worsens bias in 50\% of $K{=}2$ configurations (260/520, excluding $\Delta\pi{=}0$), with amplification reaching 2.86$\times$ ($K{=}2$) and 2.41$\times$ ($K{=}4$); Figure~\ref{fig:heatmap} visualizes the amplification surface.
Beyond amplification, global correction reverses the sign of estimated CATE---concluding a protective treatment is harmful---in 14.9\% of configurations at $\tau(0) = 0.03$ (31\% at $\tau(0) = 0.01$; critical threshold $\tau(0) < 0.089$, matching Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}), with all eight real LLMs amplifying bias under global correction; EC-HTE eliminates sign reversal entirely (Figure~\ref{fig:sign_reversal}; Appendix~\ref{app:policy_reversal}).

\subsection{Correction Evaluation}
\label{sec:ec_hte_eval}

Table~\ref{tab:main_results} presents the main results across representative configurations.
In the $K{=}2$ extreme row, global correction \emph{increases} $|\text{bias}|$ relative to naive (0.059 vs.\ 0.058), confirming the over-correction mechanism of Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}.
F-L scalar correction increases $|\text{bias}|$ to 0.122 (coverage 0.68); F-L per-subgroup to 0.168 as $(1{-}2\pi_s) \to 0$---both worse than naive (Table~\ref{tab:main_results}).
HB EC-HTE reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.059 to 0.008 (7.4$\times$); relative to stratified MLE (0.012), the advantage is 1.5$\times$ with lower RMSE from partial pooling. At $K{=}4$, bias reduces from 0.056 to 0.012 (4.7$\times$), maintaining near-nominal coverage (0.94--0.96).
Under moderate heterogeneity and in TweetEval ($K{=}4$), methods converge ($p > 0.05$); EC-HTE incurs higher RMSE when $\Delta\pi$ is small (Table~\ref{tab:main_supp}).
At $K{=}8$ ($n_{\text{expert}}/K{=}31$), coverage remains $\geq$95.6\% but RMSE increases; we recommend $n_{\text{expert}}/K \geq 50$ (Appendix~\ref{app:k8_subgroups}).

\paragraph{CausalForest.}
Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} applies to any estimator whose inputs pass through a confusion matrix; CausalForest~\cite{wager2018causal} with a noisy effect modifier $\hat{Z}$ inherits the same $M_{\text{global}}^{-1} M_s$ structure.
With CausalForest ($K{=}4$, extreme, $n{=}500$), EC-HTE reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.191 to 0.039 (4.9$\times$) with coverage 0.90; global amplifies bias up to 5.9$\times$ (Table~\ref{tab:main_results}; bootstrap SE in Appendix~\ref{app:bootstrap_se}).
The identity and correction are estimator-agnostic: R-learner yields comparable bias reduction (89\%, Appendix~\ref{app:rlearner}), confirming that the product-form bias arises from the confusion matrix structure, not the downstream estimator.

\end{table}

\subsection{Actionable Diagnostic}
\label{sec:diagnostic}

Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts} provides a $\Delta\tau$-free diagnostic: global correction increases bias in subgroup $s$ iff $|\delta_s| / ((1-2\bar{\pi}) \cdot \pi_s) > 1$, computable from a pilot sample without estimating treatment effects.
The diagnostic achieves AUC $= 0.63$ across 16 semi-synthetic LLM--dataset combinations; restricting to subgroups with $\Delta\tau > 0$ recovers AUC $= 1.0$ ($0.86$ on synthetic grids; Figure~\ref{fig:roc}, Appendix~\ref{app:screening}).
The lower AUC reflects inclusion of subgroups with $\Delta\tau \approx 0$, where misdiagnosis is inconsequential---global and stratified correction perform identically when effect heterogeneity is absent.
For $K{=}2$, $|\delta_0|{=}|\delta_1|$ limits discrimination (Appendix~\ref{app:screening}).

The condition number $\kappa(\hat{C}_s)$ provides a practical guard: $\kappa > 100$ triggers fallback; all 13 tested LLM--dataset combinations fall in $\kappa \in (1.25, 3]$ with calibrated coverage $\geq$93\% (Appendix~\ref{app:kappa_analysis}).
Budget crossover, $K{=}8$ scalability, and multi-LLM validation ($R^2 = 0.975$) appear in Appendices~\ref{sec:budget}--\ref{app:multilm}.

On a real hate speech dataset ($\Delta\pi{=}0.117$; Appendix~\ref{app:hatespeech}), EC-HTE underperforms both naive and global correction, consistent with most real LLMs exhibiting $\Delta\pi \in [0.10, 0.20]$ (Appendices~\ref{app:multilm}--\ref{app:civilcomments}).

\paragraph{Operating conditions.}
EC-HTE requires: (i)~$\Delta\pi > 0.15$, (ii)~$n_{\text{expert}} \geq 250$ for $K{=}2$, (iii)~$\text{FNR}_s < 0.50$, and (iv)~$K \leq 4$; when unmet, global correction is preferable (Appendix~\ref{app:k8_subgroups}).
Under confounded treatment, pairing with IPW-DIM maintains $\geq$94.5\% coverage (Appendix~\ref{app:confounded_dgp}).

1	\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}
2	
3	Standard confusion-matrix correction---the default in PPI, DSL, and CSS practice---can reverse causal conclusions when misclassification rates vary across subgroups.
4	We derived an exact bias identity explaining when and why, verified across synthetic grids and semi-synthetic evaluations using 11 empirical LLM confusion matrices.
5	The identity yields a diagnostic that flags harmful correction from error rates alone, and prescribes per-subgroup correction that eliminates sign reversal given sufficient error heterogeneity; when these conditions are not met, practitioners should prefer global correction.
6	The framework applies wherever LLM annotations replace structured covariates and annotation error rates vary across subpopulations.

\subsection{Stance Detection: Cross-Task Sign Reversal Validation}
\label{app:stance}

To test whether global correction introduces sign reversals beyond sentiment and toxicity, we extend the semi-synthetic evaluation to stance detection using TweetEval~\cite{barbieri2020tweeteval}.
The binary label is \emph{favor} ($Z{=}1$) vs.\ \emph{not-favor} ($Z{=}0$) toward five stance targets (Atheism, Climate Change, Feminist Movement, Hillary Clinton, Abortion), yielding $K{=}5$ subgroups with $n{=}300$ each.
CATE heterogeneity is $\tau(\text{favor}){=}0.20$, $\tau(\text{not-favor}){=}0.05$, with 200 MC replications.
GPT-4o annotations are from the real API; GPT-4o-mini and GPT-3.5-Turbo use simulated error profiles (FPR/FNR scaling $+$ additive shift; see Appendix~\ref{app:dgp}).

Table~\ref{tab:stance_signrev} reports subgroups with sign reversal or $\kappa > 3$.
Global correction produces sign reversals in 4/30 subgroup-$z$ combinations (13.3\%); EC-HTE reduces this to 1/30 (3.3\%); the remaining reversal occurs in an ill-conditioned subgroup ($\kappa{=}15.0$, GPT-3.5-Turbo Climate Change) that violates the operating conditions of Section~\ref{sec:ec_hte_eval}.
Global correction amplifies bias in 15/30 cases (50\%).

The stance task exposes an operating-conditions limitation: GPT-3.5-Turbo achieves FNR ${>}\,0.50$ on all five targets, violating the classifier quality precondition and producing $\kappa$ values up to 15.0 (Climate Change) vs.\ 4.6 (Hillary Clinton)---a ${\sim}10{\times}$ range within the same LLM.
This $\kappa$ heterogeneity inflates correction variance; EC-HTE preserves sign correctness but at the cost of higher variance when $\kappa \gg 3$.
Mean RMSE: naive${=}0.116$, global${=}0.272$, EC-HTE${=}0.271$; correction reduces sign reversals but does not improve overall RMSE at $K{=}5$, $n{=}300$ per subgroup---consistent with the operating-conditions threshold $n_{\text{expert}}/K \geq 50$.
Practitioners should verify per-subgroup FNR before applying correction.

1	\section*{Limitations}
2	\label{sec:limitations}
3	
4	Per-subgroup correction requires $n_{\text{expert}} \times P(Z_{\text{minority}}) / K \geq 25$ expert labels per subgroup and moderate classifier accuracy ($\text{FPR}_s, \text{FNR}_s < 0.5$); below these thresholds, stratification incurs more variance than the bias it removes.
5	At $K{=}8$ with $n_{\text{expert}}{=}250$ (${\approx}31$ labels/subgroup), coverage remains nominal ($\geq$95.6\%) but RMSE exceeds global correction, establishing a scalability boundary under fixed expert budget (Appendix~\ref{app:k8_subgroups}).
6	The diagnostic (Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts}) achieves AUC $= 0.86$ on synthetic data but degrades to $0.63$ on real LLM confusion matrices (Appendix~\ref{app:screening}); it should be paired with $R^2$ validation of the bias identity rather than used as a standalone rule.
7	
8	Assumption~(A1)---conditional independence of misclassification and potential outcomes---is not empirically testable.
9	Sensitivity analysis shows robustness up to $\gamma = 0.2$ for outcome-dependent misclassification (coverage $\geq$93.5\%; Appendix~\ref{app:a1_sensitivity}) and $\gamma_T \leq 0.05$ for treatment-dependent misclassification (coverage $\geq$89.7\%; Appendix~\ref{app:treatment_dep}).
10	
11	The method requires discrete, pre-specified subgroups; continuous effect modifiers require discretization, and data-driven subgroup discovery risks overfitting.
12	Ground-truth subgroup CATEs are unavailable in public datasets---classic causal inference benchmarks lack the LLM annotation step that creates the measurement error we address---so we use synthetic CATE injection on real text features and real LLM annotations (Appendices~\ref{app:dgp},~\ref{app:multilm}).
13	Code and data generation scripts will be released upon acceptance.
14

file.content:
\section*{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

Per-subgroup correction requires $n_{\text{expert}} \times P(Z_{\text{minority}}) / K \geq 25$ expert labels per subgroup and moderate classifier accuracy ($\text{FPR}_s, \text{FNR}_s < 0.5$); below these thresholds, stratification incurs more variance than the bias it removes.
At $K{=}8$ with $n_{\text{expert}}{=}250$ (${\approx}31$ labels/subgroup), coverage remains nominal ($\geq$95.6\%) but RMSE exceeds global correction, establishing a scalability boundary under fixed expert budget (Appendix~\ref{app:k8_subgroups}).
The diagnostic (Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts}) achieves AUC $= 0.86$ on synthetic data but degrades to $0.63$ on real LLM confusion matrices (Appendix~\ref{app:screening}); it should be paired with $R^2$ validation of the bias identity rather than used as a standalone rule.

Assumption~(A1)---conditional independence of misclassification and potential outcomes---is not empirically testable.
Sensitivity analysis shows robustness up to $\gamma = 0.2$ for outcome-dependent misclassification (coverage $\geq$93.5\%; Appendix~\ref{app:a1_sensitivity}) and $\gamma_T \leq 0.05$ for treatment-dependent misclassification (coverage $\geq$89.7\%; Appendix~\ref{app:treatment_dep}).

The method requires discrete, pre-specified subgroups; continuous effect modifiers require discretization, and data-driven subgroup discovery risks overfitting.
Ground-truth subgroup CATEs are unavailable in public datasets---classic causal inference benchmarks lack the LLM annotation step that creates the measurement error we address---so we use synthetic CATE injection on real text features and real LLM annotations (Appendices~\ref{app:dgp},~\ref{app:multilm}).
Code and data generation scripts will be released upon acceptance.

410	Low-error subgroups ($s_0$--$s_1$) benefit from stratification, with HB RMSE 14--25\% below global correction.
411	HB partial pooling reduces MLE RMSE by 24--54\% in the high-$\pi$ regime ($s_4$--$s_7$), confirming that hierarchical shrinkage provides meaningful regularization even when per-subgroup labels are scarce.
412	Coverage remains $\geq$0.94 across all subgroups for HB EC-HTE, indicating that variance inflation does not compromise inference validity.
413	Adaptive shrinkage---increasing the prior strength for high-$\pi$ subgroups where CM estimation is least reliable---is a natural extension that may close the RMSE gap with global correction at larger $K$.
414	
415	We explored adaptive shrinkage ($\alpha{=}10$ for high-$\pi$ subgroups vs.\ default $\alpha{=}3$), which reduces aggregate RMSE from 0.340 to 0.216 (35\% improvement) by attenuating estimation noise in high-$\pi$ subgroups.
416	However, RMSE remains 30\% above global correction (0.166), confirming that the bottleneck is per-subgroup sample size (${\sim}$31 expert labels) rather than the shrinkage method itself.
417	This establishes $K{=}8$ at $n_{\text{expert}}{=}250$ as a boundary condition: all correction methods provide valid inference (coverage $\geq$94\%), but per-subgroup stratification requires proportionally larger expert budgets---approximately $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 500$ (${\approx}60$ labels/subgroup)---to achieve RMSE parity with global correction.
418	
419	\section{Asymmetric Misclassification Extension}
420	\label{app:asymmetric}
421	
422	Assumption~(A2) imposes symmetric misclassification ($\text{FPR}_s = \text{FNR}_s = \pi_s$), which simplifies the bias decomposition but is not necessary for it.
423	Real LLM annotators typically exhibit asymmetric confusion patterns; we show here that the product structure generalizes.
424	
425	\paragraph{General bias formula.}
426	For asymmetric confusion matrices $C_s = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix} 1{-}\text{FPR}_s & \text{FPR}_s \\ \text{FNR}_s & 1{-}\text{FNR}_s \end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$, define the mixing matrix $M_s$ via Bayesian inversion and the residual matrix $B_s = M_{\text{global}}^{-1} M_s - I$.
427	Since both $M_s$ and $M_{\text{global}}$ are row-stochastic, $B_s \mathbf{1} = \mathbf{0}$.
428	Decomposing $\boldsymbol{\tau} = \tau(0)\mathbf{1} + \Delta\tau \, \mathbf{e}_1$ gives:
429	\begin{equation}
430	\text{bias}(z, s) = \Delta\tau \cdot [B_s]_{z,1},
431	\end{equation}
432	where $[B_s]_{z,1}$ depends only on $\{\text{FPR}_k, \text{FNR}_k, w_k\}$, not on $\Delta\tau$.
433	Under~(A2), this reduces to $\delta_s \Delta\tau / (1 - 2\bar{\pi})$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}).
434	
435	\paragraph{Empirical validation.}
436	We test three asymmetric configurations ($K{=}2$, $n_{\text{expert}}{=}250$, 100 MC runs each): \emph{Cross} (FPR/FNR = 0.10/0.20 vs.\ 0.25/0.10), \emph{Co-directional} (0.05/0.15 vs.\ 0.20/0.30), and \emph{Extreme} (0.03/0.25 vs.\ 0.30/0.05).
437	Regressing analytic predictions on MC bias yields $R^2 = 0.991$ across all configurations, confirming the product structure under asymmetry.
438	Table~\ref{tab:asymmetric} reports correction performance averaged over subgroups, $z$-levels, and $\Delta\tau \in \{0.1, \ldots, 0.5\}$.
439	EC-HTE reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.025 (global) to 0.006, a $4\times$ improvement, with lower RMSE (0.033 vs.\ 0.040) and substantially better coverage (0.90 vs.\ 0.78).

534	\section{Real-Data Case Study: Hate Speech Detection}
535	\label{app:hatespeech}
536	
537	We apply EC-HTE to the UC Berkeley Measuring Hate Speech corpus~\cite{kennedy2020constructing}, annotating 2{,}496 comments for dehumanization using GPT-4.1.
538	Four text-feature subgroups are defined by crossing platform (Reddit/Gab vs.\ Twitter/YouTube) and text length (above/below median), yielding balanced groups ($n \approx 624$ each).
539	
540	\paragraph{Positive finding: real-world heterogeneity.}
541	Per-subgroup misclassification rates range from 0.266 to 0.383, confirming heterogeneity ($\Delta\pi = 0.117$) in a real annotation setting.
542	At the error-type level, FPR ranges from 8.5\% to 21.3\% across text-feature subgroups, demonstrating that subgroup-varying misclassification is not an artifact of synthetic design but arises naturally in real NLP annotation tasks.
543	
544	\paragraph{Boundary condition: statistical power at extreme FNR.}
545	Correction results are inconclusive: all corrected confidence intervals contain zero, and point estimate differences between methods are not statistically significant.
546	The high baseline FNR (53.3\%) amplifies variance through matrix inversion (variance amplification factor up to 15.7$\times$), rendering the comparison underpowered.
547	When $P(\hat{Z}{=}1 \mid Z{=}1) \approx 0.5$, the confusion matrix approaches singularity, and inversion amplifies estimation noise regardless of stratification strategy.
548	This complements the expert budget threshold identified in Appendix~\ref{sec:budget}: EC-HTE requires \emph{both} sufficient expert labels \emph{and} sufficient baseline classifier quality.
549	
550	\paragraph{Diagnostic connection.}
551	The diagnostic criterion ($\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$, Section~\ref{sec:diagnostic}) identifies when correction is worthwhile under moderate baseline accuracy.
552	This case study illustrates that even when $\Delta\pi$ is large, extreme baseline error renders correction underpowered rather than beneficial.
553	A practical prerequisite is that the per-subgroup confusion matrix condition number $\kappa(\hat{C}_s)$ remain moderate; when $\kappa > 50$, as observed here, practitioners should prioritize improving annotation quality before applying any matrix-inversion-based correction.

796	When both conditions hold, HB outperforms global in 93.3\% of cells; when either is violated, global is preferred in 94.7\% of cells.
797	Both exp-015 ($\kappa = 2.38$, effective $n = 2.5$) and exp-016 ($\kappa = 1.55$, effective $n = 2.5$) violate both conditions, and the diagnostic correctly predicts 100\% of their failure cells.

We explored adaptive shrinkage ($\alpha{=}10$ for high-$\pi$ subgroups vs.\ default $\alpha{=}3$), which reduces aggregate RMSE from 0.340 to 0.216 (35\% improvement) by attenuating estimation noise in high-$\pi$ subgroups.
However, RMSE remains 30\% above global correction (0.166), confirming that the bottleneck is per-subgroup sample size (${\sim}$31 expert labels) rather than the shrinkage method itself.
This establishes $K{=}8$ at $n_{\text{expert}}{=}250$ as a boundary condition: all correction methods provide valid inference (coverage $\geq$94\%), but per-subgroup stratification requires proportionally larger expert budgets---approximately $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 500$ (${\approx}60$ labels/subgroup)---to achieve RMSE parity with global correction.

\section{Asymmetric Misclassification Extension}
\label{app:asymmetric}

Assumption~(A2) imposes symmetric misclassification ($\text{FPR}_s = \text{FNR}_s = \pi_s$), which simplifies the bias decomposition but is not necessary for it.
Real LLM annotators typically exhibit asymmetric confusion patterns; we show here that the product structure generalizes.

\paragraph{General bias formula.}
For asymmetric confusion matrices $C_s = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix} 1{-}\text{FPR}_s & \text{FPR}_s \\ \text{FNR}_s & 1{-}\text{FNR}_s \end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$, define the mixing matrix $M_s$ via Bayesian inversion and the residual matrix $B_s = M_{\text{global}}^{-1} M_s - I$.
Since both $M_s$ and $M_{\text{global}}$ are row-stochastic, $B_s \mathbf{1} = \mathbf{0}$.
Decomposing $\boldsymbol{\tau} = \tau(0)\mathbf{1} + \Delta\tau \, \mathbf{e}_1$ gives:
\begin{equation}
\text{bias}(z, s) = \Delta\tau \cdot [B_s]_{z,1},
\end{equation}
where $[B_s]_{z,1}$ depends only on $\{\text{FPR}_k, \text{FNR}_k, w_k\}$, not on $\Delta\tau$.
Under~(A2), this reduces to $\delta_s \Delta\tau / (1 - 2\bar{\pi})$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}).

\paragraph{Empirical validation.}
We test three asymmetric configurations ($K{=}2$, $n_{\text{expert}}{=}250$, 100 MC runs each): \emph{Cross} (FPR/FNR = 0.10/0.20 vs.\ 0.25/0.10), \emph{Co-directional} (0.05/0.15 vs.\ 0.20/0.30), and \emph{Extreme} (0.03/0.25 vs.\ 0.30/0.05).
Regressing analytic predictions on MC bias yields $R^2 = 0.991$ across all configurations, confirming the product structure under asymmetry.
Table~\ref{tab:asymmetric} reports correction performance averaged over subgroups, $z$-levels, and $\Delta\tau \in \{0.1, \ldots, 0.5\}$.
EC-HTE reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.025 (global) to 0.006, a $4\times$ improvement, with lower RMSE (0.033 vs.\ 0.040) and substantially better coverage (0.90 vs.\ 0.78).

\section{Real-Data Case Study: Hate Speech Detection}
\label{app:hatespeech}

We apply EC-HTE to the UC Berkeley Measuring Hate Speech corpus~\cite{kennedy2020constructing}, annotating 2{,}496 comments for dehumanization using GPT-4.1.
Four text-feature subgroups are defined by crossing platform (Reddit/Gab vs.\ Twitter/YouTube) and text length (above/below median), yielding balanced groups ($n \approx 624$ each).

\paragraph{Positive finding: real-world heterogeneity.}
Per-subgroup misclassification rates range from 0.266 to 0.383, confirming heterogeneity ($\Delta\pi = 0.117$) in a real annotation setting.
At the error-type level, FPR ranges from 8.5\% to 21.3\% across text-feature subgroups, demonstrating that subgroup-varying misclassification is not an artifact of synthetic design but arises naturally in real NLP annotation tasks.

\paragraph{Boundary condition: statistical power at extreme FNR.}
Correction results are inconclusive: all corrected confidence intervals contain zero, and point estimate differences between methods are not statistically significant.
The high baseline FNR (53.3\%) amplifies variance through matrix inversion (variance amplification factor up to 15.7$\times$), rendering the comparison underpowered.
When $P(\hat{Z}{=}1 \mid Z{=}1) \approx 0.5$, the confusion matrix approaches singularity, and inversion amplifies estimation noise regardless of stratification strategy.
This complements the expert budget threshold identified in Appendix~\ref{sec:budget}: EC-HTE requires \emph{both} sufficient expert labels \emph{and} sufficient baseline classifier quality.

\paragraph{Diagnostic connection.}
The diagnostic criterion ($\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$, Section~\ref{sec:diagnostic}) identifies when correction is worthwhile under moderate baseline accuracy.
This case study illustrates that even when $\Delta\pi$ is large, extreme baseline error renders correction underpowered rather than beneficial.
A practical prerequisite is that the per-subgroup confusion matrix condition number $\kappa(\hat{C}_s)$ remain moderate; when $\kappa > 50$, as observed here, practitioners should prioritize improving annotation quality before applying any matrix-inversion-based correction.

The singularity guard ($\kappa > 100$, Section~\ref{sec:method}) mitigates catastrophic failure by falling back to global correction for near-degenerate subgroups, but does not recover the bias reduction that motivates stratification.
For a $2 \times 2$ symmetric confusion matrix, $\kappa = 1/|1-2\pi|$; $\kappa > 100$ corresponds to $\pi \in (0.495, 0.505)$, so the guard triggers only when the classifier performs within $0.5\%$ of random guessing.

Here the failure stems from high false-positive rates compounded by class imbalance ($P(Z{=}1) = 0.18$), which leaves insufficient expert observations in the positive class for reliable per-subgroup confusion matrix estimation.
Together, these experiments identify three applicability conditions for EC-HTE: (1)~sufficient effective expert budget ($n_{\text{expert}} \times P(Z_{\text{minority}}) / K \geq 25$), (2)~no near-chance subgroup error rate ($\max(\text{FPR}_s, \text{FNR}_s) < 0.5$), and (3)~adequate class balance in the effect modifier.

\paragraph{Diagnostic rule.}

896	\section{Comparison with PPI Correction}
897	\label{app:ppi_comparison}
898	
899	PPI~\cite{angelopoulos2023ppi} constructs confidence intervals by combining a large set of ML predictions with a smaller set of gold-standard labels, using the gold labels to debias the ML-based estimator.
900	Applied to our setting, PPI treats the LLM-annotated effect modifier as the ML prediction and the expert labels as the gold standard.
901	Two variants arise naturally: \emph{PPI-global} pools all expert labels to estimate a single rectifier (analogous to our Global baseline), and \emph{PPI-subgroup} estimates per-subgroup rectifiers (analogous to Stratified MLE).
902	
903	Under the confusion-matrix parameterization we adopt, DSL's measurement error correction reduces to confusion matrix inversion.
904	Pooled DSL applies a single estimated confusion matrix to all subgroups, producing the same corrected label distribution as our Global baseline; per-subgroup DSL estimates a separate confusion matrix for each subgroup and inverts it independently, equivalent to our Stratified MLE.
905	EC-HTE's contribution over both PPI-subgroup and per-subgroup DSL is hierarchical partial pooling: rather than estimating each subgroup's confusion matrix in isolation, EC-HTE places a shared prior across subgroups, borrowing strength to reduce variance while preserving subgroup-specific bias correction.
906	This mechanism is outside both the PPI and DSL frameworks.
907	
908	The key difference between PPI and confusion-matrix inversion is that PPI does not invert the confusion matrix; instead, it uses the gold labels to directly debias the estimand.
909	This avoids the matrix inversion step that can amplify noise at small $n_{\text{expert}}$, but it also means PPI cannot exploit the structure of the misclassification process to reduce bias.
910	PPI-global inherits the same $\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$ bias amplification as Global correction (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}), confirming that the ``debiasing hurts'' mechanism operates regardless of the inference framework.

\section{Comparison with PPI Correction}
\label{app:ppi_comparison}

PPI~\cite{angelopoulos2023ppi} constructs confidence intervals by combining a large set of ML predictions with a smaller set of gold-standard labels, using the gold labels to debias the ML-based estimator.
Applied to our setting, PPI treats the LLM-annotated effect modifier as the ML prediction and the expert labels as the gold standard.
Two variants arise naturally: \emph{PPI-global} pools all expert labels to estimate a single rectifier (analogous to our Global baseline), and \emph{PPI-subgroup} estimates per-subgroup rectifiers (analogous to Stratified MLE).

Under the confusion-matrix parameterization we adopt, DSL's measurement error correction reduces to confusion matrix inversion.
Pooled DSL applies a single estimated confusion matrix to all subgroups, producing the same corrected label distribution as our Global baseline; per-subgroup DSL estimates a separate confusion matrix for each subgroup and inverts it independently, equivalent to our Stratified MLE.
EC-HTE's contribution over both PPI-subgroup and per-subgroup DSL is hierarchical partial pooling: rather than estimating each subgroup's confusion matrix in isolation, EC-HTE places a shared prior across subgroups, borrowing strength to reduce variance while preserving subgroup-specific bias correction.
This mechanism is outside both the PPI and DSL frameworks.

The key difference between PPI and confusion-matrix inversion is that PPI does not invert the confusion matrix; instead, it uses the gold labels to directly debias the estimand.
This avoids the matrix inversion step that can amplify noise at small $n_{\text{expert}}$, but it also means PPI cannot exploit the structure of the misclassification process to reduce bias.
PPI-global inherits the same $\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$ bias amplification as Global correction (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}), confirming that the ``debiasing hurts'' mechanism operates regardless of the inference framework.

\section{Civil Comments Validation}
\label{app:civilcomments}

To verify that subgroup-heterogeneous misclassification generalizes beyond TweetEval, we annotate $N{=}3{,}000$ stratified samples (30\% toxic) from Civil Comments~\cite{borkan2019nuanced}, a toxicity detection dataset.
Subgroups are defined by \texttt{text\_length\_bin} $\times$ \texttt{has\_question} ($K{=}4$): S0 (long, no question, 38.8\%), S1 (long, question, 11.4\%), S2 (short, no question, 33.7\%), S3 (short, question, 16.1\%).
Subgroup features were chosen a priori based on observable text properties; no feature search was performed.
Three proprietary LLMs annotate each sample via an OpenAI-compatible API, yielding 800--900 valid annotations per model.

Table~\ref{tab:civil_cm} reports per-subgroup FPR and FNR.
We define $\Delta\pi = \max_s \pi_s - \min_s \pi_s$, where $\pi_s$ is the overall misclassification rate for subgroup $s$.
All three models exhibit $\Delta\pi > 0.05$, with overall heterogeneity $\Delta\pi \in [0.113, 0.160]$---comparable to the $\Delta\pi \in [0.125, 0.165]$ observed across four open-source LLMs on TweetEval (Appendix~\ref{app:multilm_opensource}).
